Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 47 min read (9306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~47 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges1.
  • In a recent development, photoconversion processes underpin technologies ranging from photodetection and photovoltaics to photoemission and photochemistry.
  • Sources indicate that recent studies have shown that hot carriers can be manipulated using ultrafast spin exchange (SE) interactions in manganese (Mn)-doped colloidal quantum dots (QDs)10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges1. Here we demonstrate a spin-exchange-driven phototransport regime in manganese-doped quantum dot films that enables the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers. Ultrafast spin-exchange-mediated Auger upconversion promotes electrons into high-energy, delocalized states before phonon cooling2,3, establishing a transient high-mobility conduction channel. Crucially, spin-exchange interactions not only generate hot carriers but also enable their repeated re-excitation, thereby sustaining long-range drift. This mechanism yields room-temperature mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre drift lengths—far greater than those of conventional quantum dot solids and approaching values characteristic of crystalline semiconductors. Time-of-flight measurements confirm drift-dominated transport, with transit times scaling linearly with distance and inversely with electric field. These results establish a route to long-range energy transport in nanoscale materials and enable the use of hot carriers in photoconversion, photochemistry and transit-time-limited photodetection.

In a recent development, photoconversion processes underpin technologies ranging from photodetection and photovoltaics to photoemission and photochemistry. Their ability to exploit excess photon energy is limited by rapid phonon-assisted cooling of nonequilibrium (‘hot’) carriers to band-edge states, typically within picoseconds, severely restricting their lifetime and transport range. Stabilizing and transporting hot carriers therefore remains a substantial challenge for advanced solar-energy conversion4,5,6,7 and high-energy photochemistry8,9.

Sources indicate that recent studies have shown that hot carriers can be manipulated using ultrafast spin exchange (SE) interactions in manganese (Mn)-doped colloidal quantum dots (QDs)10,11,12. These interactions mediate subpicosecond Auger-type energy transfer between QD excitons and Mn spin states, reaching energy-transfer rates of about 10 eV ps−1 (ref. 11), well above typical phonon-related energy-loss rates (≲1 eV ps−1)13,14. By outcompeting intraband cooling, SE-Auger processes provide an efficient pathway for harvesting hot-electron energy, enabling phenomena such as visible-light generation of solvated electrons2,15 and carrier multiplication12.

Industry observers note that here we demonstrate that SE-Auger upconversion in Mn-doped QD films promotes photoelectrons into high-energy, delocalized transport states, enabling rapid, long-range hot-carrier transport through the QD solid. Transient photocurrent (TPC) measurements reveal time-of-flight (ToF) dynamics with drift mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre transport distances—well beyond those typically observed in QD solids. These results establish a route to long-range hot-carrier transport for photoconversion and hot-electron-driven photochemistry.

We prepared undoped (reference) and Mn-doped CdSe QDs overcoated with a thin protective CdS shell (Methods). We focus on CdSe/CdS QDs with an initial core radius of rCdSe ≈ 1.65 nm. The undoped sample exhibits a photoluminescence (PL) peak at about 2.15 eV and a band-edge (1S) absorption feature at about 2.23 eV (Fig. 1a, black curves).

Sources indicate that a, Absorption (solid lines) and PL (dashed lines) spectra of undoped (black), lightly doped (blue) and heavily doped (red) QDs. The orange arrow marks the internal Mn spin-flip transition (EMn = 2.1 eV). Insets, schematics of undoped (top), lightly doped (middle) and heavily doped (bottom) CdSe/CdS QDs. In the heavily doped sample, an interfacial MnxCd1−xSe barrier layer forms between the CdSe core and CdS shell. b, PL dynamics of undoped (black), lightly doped (blue) and heavily doped (red) QDs. Single-exponential fits to the undoped and lightly doped traces (dashed lines) yield τPL,0 = 35 ns and τPL,Mn = 61 ns, respectively; a double-exponential fit to the heavily doped trace (dashed red line) gives an average lifetime of ⟨τPL,Mn⟩ = 225 ns. Inset, forward (time constant τF, solid black arrows) and backward (τB, dashed black arrows) SE-driven excitation transfer between the QD exciton and Mn spin excitation. Short red arrows indicate the spin orientation of electrons (filled red circles); for holes (open red circles), the arrow denotes the spin of the electron removed to create the hole. c, Tail-normalized band-edge bleach dynamics of the undoped sample as a function of ⟨N⟩, the average number of excitons generated per QD per pulse; ΔαBE is the pump-induced change in the band-edge absorption coefficient. At ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, a fast component emerges owing to multiexciton Auger recombination, illustrated in the bottom inset for a biexciton (XX). Top inset, biexciton dynamics obtained by subtracting tail-normalized traces measured at ⟨N⟩ = 1.32 and 0.19 (circles); a single-exponential fit (line) gives τA = 85 ps. d, Corresponding dynamics for lightly doped QDs show strongly accelerated decay owing to SE-Auger recombination (note the 8-ps time window compared with 800 ps in c). The SE-Auger lifetimes of hybrid biexciton (X–Mn*) and triexciton (XX–Mn*) states, extracted using the subtraction procedure (top inset), are τSE-A = 0.91 ps and 0.23 ps, respectively. The SE-Auger process is illustrated in the bottom inset. All measurements were performed on QD solutions in toluene; time-resolved PL and TA measurements used 150-fs, 2.4-eV excitation pulses. a.u., arbitrary units.

Recent findings suggest that mn-doped samples were synthesized by diffusion doping of the CdSe cores, involving partial Cd2+ → Mn2+ cation exchange near the surface followed by Mn diffusion into the core interior16,17 (Methods). The Mn content was controlled by the doping time (tMn = 5–30 min). Here we examine samples prepared with tMn = 10 and 20 min, referred to as ‘lightly’ and ‘heavily’ doped QDs, respectively.

The lightly doped QDs show spectral features similar to those of the undoped reference (Fig. 1a, blue curves), indicating no appreciable change in the effective CdSe core size. The heavily doped sample exhibits an approximately 130-meV blue shift of both PL and absorption (Fig. 1a, red curves), consistent with a reduction of the effective CdSe core radius to about 1.35 nm owing to formation of a higher-bandgap MnxCd1−xSe surface layer.

According to recent reports, mn incorporation strongly modifies single-exciton PL dynamics measured at low excitation levels (⟨N⟩ < 0.1, in which ⟨N⟩ is the average number of excitons generated per QD per pulse). The PL lifetime increases from τPL,0 = 35 ns in undoped QDs to τPL,Mn = 61 ns in lightly doped QDs and to an average of 225 ns in heavily doped QDs (Fig. 1b).

Recent findings suggest that this behaviour arises from ultrafast (subpicosecond) bidirectional SE-mediated excitation transfer between the QD exciton (X) and the internal Mn spin-flip transition (EMn = 2.1 eV)2,10,18. In the forward process, the QD exciton relaxes while promoting the Mn ion from the spin-up 6A1 ground state to the spin-down 4T1 state (Fig. 1b, inset). This occurs through two concerted spin-conserving transfers: a spin-up Mn 3d electron fills the QD valence-band (VB) hole, while a spin-down QD conduction-band (CB) electron is simultaneously transferred into the Mn 3d shell. In the reverse process, spin-flip relaxation of the excited Mn ion (Mn*) regenerates a QD exciton.

The rapid forward and backward transfers establish a quasi-steady-state distribution between excitonic and Mn-based states, with occupation probabilities pX and pMn related by pX/pMn = exp[−(ΕX − ΕMn)/δ0], in which ΕX is the exciton energy (determined from the PL peak energy) and δ0 = 103 meV is an experimentally determined characteristic energy3,11. Because the intrinsic Mn* lifetime is very long (τMn ≳ 1 ms; ref. 18), decay of the coupled X–Mn system is governed by its excitonic component, 1/τPL,Mn ≈ pX/τPL,0.

In a recent development, for the lightly doped sample, in which EMn ≈ EX, pX ≈ pMn, giving τPL,Mn ≈ 2τPL,0 ≈ 70 ns, close to the measured 61 ns. For the heavily doped sample (ΕX − ΕMn = 188 meV), the model yields τPL,Mn ≈ 7.2τPL,0 ≈ 252 ns, again close to the observed 225 ns. The prolonged lifetime of the coupled X–Mn excitation facilitates multiexciton formation and thereby supports the SE-Auger processes underlying the long-range hot-electron transport discussed below.

Industry observers note that although slowing single-exciton decay, Mn doping greatly accelerates multiexciton dynamics, which in undoped QDs are governed by Auger recombination, for which electron–hole recombination energy is transferred to a third carrier within the same QD19 (Fig. 1c, bottom inset). In the undoped sample, this process appears as a fast decay component in transient absorption (TA) traces (Methods), emerging near ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 (Fig. 1c). From this component, we extract a biexciton Auger lifetime of τA = 85 ps (Fig. 1c, top inset).

In Mn-doped QDs, the TA decay also accelerates near ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 (Fig. 1d, lightly doped sample), but the corresponding time constant is nearly two orders of magnitude shorter, about 910 fs, and decreases further to about 230 fs at higher excitation levels (Fig. 1d, top inset). These subpicosecond dynamics arise from SE-Auger recombination of hybrid multiexciton states comprising intrinsic QD excitons and excited Mn ions2,3. In the electron re-excitation pathway (Fig. 1d, bottom inset), two concerted spin-transfer events promote a spin-down Mn 3d electron into a hot QD CB state, whereas the Mn ion is restored to its ground-state configuration by transfer of a spin-up electron from the QD band-edge CB state. As a result, the hot electron is elevated above the QD band edge by EMn.

Previous studies established that the SE-Auger rate depends mainly on exciton multiplicity and only weakly on the number of excited Mn ions3. Accordingly, the observed time constants of 910 and 230 fs are consistent with SE-Auger decay of hybrid biexciton (X–Mn*) and triexciton (XX–Mn*) states, respectively3.

In a recent development, A key consequence is the very high energy-gain rate associated with SE-Auger upconversion (rgain). For τSE-A = 230 fs, rgain = rSE-A = EMn/τSE-A ≈ 9 eV ps−1, far exceeding typical phonon-assisted energy-loss rates (rphon ≲ 1 eV ps−1)13,14. Thus, SE-Auger upconversion can outcompete phonon cooling and efficiently generate and manipulate hot carriers.

In a recent development, A high SE-Auger upconversion rate could enable Auger-assisted hot-carrier transport with strongly enhanced photoconductance. Specifically, theory predicts that Auger excitation above the QD ionization threshold can promote electrons into delocalized, ‘quasi-free’ states with greatly increased mobility20. Experimentally, short-lived bursts of enhanced carrier mobility were previously observed in undoped PbSe QD films21 and attributed to Auger-generated hot electrons that remained confined within individual QDs. The corresponding transport range was, however, limited to the approximately 50–100-nm near-contact region. Here we use ultrafast SE-Auger interactions to promote electrons above the confinement barrier, as originally foreseen in ref. 20, and show that this enables submillimetre transport.

The concept of Auger-enhanced conductivity is illustrated in Fig. 2a. If an electron is excited above the QD confinement barrier—that is, effectively ejected from the QD—it can access a high-mobility transport band formed by closely spaced, delocalized peripheral states22. In typical CdSe QDs, however, direct ejection of a band-edge electron by a single conventional Auger upconversion step is unfavourable because the transferred energy, approximately equal to the bandgap Eg, is smaller than the confinement barrier. Ejection can still occur from higher-lying transient states (Fig. 2a) but rapid phonon cooling usually returns carriers to the band edge before Auger upconversion can take place.

It has been revealed that a, Schematic of Auger-assisted hot-carrier photoconductance. Absorption of an above-band-edge photon (wavy blue arrow) in a QD containing a pre-existing electron generates a multicarrier (trion) state that undergoes Auger recombination, promoting an electron into a high-energy, delocalized hot state. Access to this state requires retention of the photogenerated electron’s excess energy and is therefore efficient only when the Auger energy-transfer rate (rA) exceeds the phonon-assisted energy-loss rate (rphon). b, Schematic of the Auston switch device containing a QD film as the photoactive layer (top) and the experimental geometry (bottom). The QD film within the 70-µm gap (L) between two gold (Au) electrodes is excited by a focused laser beam whose position can be translated across the gap; d denotes the distance between the beam centre and the positive electrode. c, Photocurrent transients for the undoped sample as a function of excitation level (⟨N⟩ = 0.23–5.38). Inset, tail-normalized TPC traces for ⟨N⟩ = 0.23 and 2.00 (black); their difference (red) is fitted to a single exponential, yielding a biexciton Auger lifetime of τA = 110 ps. Measurements used 150-fs, 3.6-eV excitation pulses with the beam centred at d = 15 μm. IRF denotes the instrument response function. d, TPC traces for the heavily doped sample under identical conditions exhibit markedly different behaviour at high ⟨N⟩, developing a pronounced step-like component whose amplitude increases rapidly—approximately cubically—with ⟨N⟩ (inset). a.u., arbitrary units.

According to recent reports, owing to its ultrafast character, SE-Auger upconversion can overcome this limitation by ejecting a nonthermalized electron before it loses its excess energy to phonons11. Band-edge electrons can also be expelled from the QD through two sequential SE-Auger upconversion steps2.

Industry observers note that to investigate the role of SE interactions in phototransport, we performed TPC measurements using Auston switch devices in which undoped or Mn-doped QD films were incorporated into a 70-µm gap of a 50-Ω microstrip transmission line21,23,24,25 (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1; Methods). The QDs were excited by 150-fs laser pulses focused into a narrow stripe (70–80 µm full width at half maximum, FWHM), whose position within the gap was varied by translating the sample. The TPC signal was recorded with a 20-GHz sampling oscilloscope, yielding an overall temporal resolution of approximately 50 ps.

Dark-conductivity measurements (Extended Data Fig. 2) show that the QD films are highly resistive at equilibrium, indicating that the TPC response is dominated by photogenerated rather than equilibrium carriers.

According to recent reports, in most experiments, the QDs were excited at Ephot = 3.6 eV, more than 1 eV above the band edge. Under these conditions, SE-Auger interactions can efficiently eject electrons from Mn-doped QDs11, whereas ejection by means of slower conventional Auger processes in undoped QDs is much less likely. Thus, any strong enhancement of photoconductance provides a direct signature of SE-Auger-driven hot-carrier generation and transport.

Sources indicate that in Fig. 2c,d, we compare pump-intensity-dependent photocurrent transients for undoped and Mn-doped QD films, respectively, measured at a device bias of V = 100 V and Ephot = 3.6 eV.

For the undoped sample, the excitation range corresponds to ⟨N⟩ from 0.23 to 5.38 excitons per QD. Increasing pump fluence does not substantially alter the overall TPC profile; the main effect is an acceleration of the early-time decay at ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, similar to the behaviour observed in TA measurements (Fig. 1c) and likewise indicative of multiexciton Auger recombination. A biexciton Auger lifetime extracted from the fast TPC component (about 110 ps; Fig. 2c, inset) agrees reasonably well with that obtained from TA (about 85 ps; Fig. 1c, inset).

It has been revealed that the ⟨N⟩ dependence of both the early-time TPC peak amplitude (time t = tpeak) and the long-time signal (t = 400 ps > τA) is also well described by the Auger recombination model (Fig. 3a, black symbols and lines). In this model, the peak photocurrent contains contributions from both single-exciton and multiexciton states, whereas after Auger decay, the long-time signal originates only from single excitons (Supplementary Note 1).

Recent findings suggest that a, Early-time peak TPC signal (open squares) and long-time (t = 400 ps; post-Auger decay) TPC amplitude (filled black circles) for the undoped sample as a function of ⟨N⟩, extracted from Fig. 2c. The data are described by a model assuming Poisson-distributed initial exciton occupancies and constant carrier mobility (black lines). For the doped sample, the TPC step amplitude at t = 400 ps (filled red circles; from Fig. 2d) increases rapidly for ⟨N⟩ > 1, indicating a strong increase in carrier mobility. The data are reproduced by a model of SE-Auger-assisted activation into a high-mobility hot-electron transport band (red line). b, Schematic of SE-Auger upconversion involving an electron in a transient above-band-edge state. This process competes with phonon-assisted relaxation (‘cooling’) at rate rphon. Efficient promotion of electrons into the hot-carrier transport band requires the SE-Auger energy-transfer rate rSE-A to exceed rphon. c, Early-time TA spectra of a heavily doped QD film (Ephot = 3.6 eV, Δt = 3 ps) for ⟨N⟩ ≲ 1 (green and blue) and ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1 (red and black). Below the SE-Auger onset, the spectra are dominated by the band-edge bleach from state filling. Above the onset, a pronounced photoinduced absorption develops below the bleach, producing the derivative-like lineshape characteristic of a carrier-induced Stark effect. Inset, SE-Auger activation into a delocalized transport state spatially separates the electron and hole wavefunctions, generating a local electric field (Feh, red arrow) that shifts the band-edge transition by ΔESt. a.u., arbitrary units.

Industry observers note that these results show that TPC dynamics in undoped QD films are dominated by carrier recombination, with no detectable signatures of transit across the electrode gap. The corresponding transit times are therefore much longer than the characteristic recombination times because of the low carrier mobility.

According to recent reports, in contrast to the undoped samples, photocurrent transients from Mn-doped QD films change markedly with increasing pump fluence (Fig. 2d, heavily doped sample). At ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, the TPC traces develop a pronounced step-like component whose amplitude grows approximately cubically with ⟨N⟩ (IPC,400ps ∝ ⟨N⟩3.05; Fig. 2d, inset), where IPC,400ps is the photocurrent amplitude measured at t = 400 ps after excitation. This superlinear growth cannot be explained by the increase in carrier population alone and instead indicates an increase in carrier mobility by orders of magnitude.

According to recent reports, the onset of this rapid photocurrent growth coincides with the threshold for SE-Auger recombination, suggesting SE-Auger-driven activation of electrons into a higher-energy transport band above the QD confinement barrier, as proposed in ref. 20. The absence of this effect in undoped QDs further points to the critical role of ultrafast SE-Auger upconversion, which can intercept an energetic photoelectron before intraband cooling and promote it into a peripheral, delocalized state outside the QD (Fig. 3b).

Industry observers note that the excitation-level dependence of the TPC step amplitude (evaluated at t = 400 ps) further supports its SE-Auger origin. As detailed in Supplementary Note 2, the data are well described using the previously established (n − 1)2 scaling of the SE-Auger rate with exciton multiplicity n (Fig. 3a, red symbols and line)3.

According to recent reports, further evidence for electron ejection from the QD is provided by pump-fluence-dependent TA spectra (Fig. 3c). At ⟨N⟩ < 1, the spectra are dominated by a state-filling bleach at 2.34 eV, whereas at ⟨N⟩ ≳ 1, they evolve into a derivative-like lineshape characteristic of electron ejection11,26. The resulting spatial separation of the ejected electron and the hole remaining in the QD generates an internal electric field (Fig. 3c, inset) that redshifts the band-edge transition through the Stark effect, producing induced absorption below the original bleach.

In a recent development, A step-like TPC signal with an abrupt cut-off is a hallmark of ToF photocurrent observed in high-mobility photoconductors, in which photocarriers are rapidly swept from the photoconductive gap by drift towards the electrodes27,28,29. In this regime, the photocurrent duration is determined not by carrier relaxation but by the carrier transit time, ttr = d/vd = d/(μF), in which d is the transport distance, vd the drift velocity, μ the carrier mobility and F the electric field.

To test for ToF transport in Mn-doped QD films, we measured photocurrent transients as a function of both transport distance and electric field, F = V/L, in which L = 70 μm is the electrode gap. Figure 4a highlights TPC traces for heavily doped QDs at three distances from the positive electrode, d = 15, 45 and 65 µm. The TPC pulse duration increases systematically with d, a defining signature of carrier transit27 and evidence that the photoresponse is dominated by high-mobility hot electrons generated by SE-Auger upconversion2,30,31.

It has been revealed that a, TPC traces for heavily doped QDs measured at V = 100 V, Ephot = 3.6 eV and ⟨N⟩ = 5.12 (solid lines) for d = 15 µm (red), 45 µm (blue) and 65 µm (green). Dashed lines are fits to the ToF model, yielding vd = 24 µm ns−1, 22 µm ns−1 and 13 µm ns−1, respectively, with τ0 = 7 ns. Inset, transit time as a function of d, determined from the inflection points of log–log TPC plots (symbols) for V = 100 V (red) and 70 V (black). Linear fits (lines) yield vd = 21.5 ± 0.4 µm ns−1 and 15.3 ± 0.4 µm ns−1, respectively. b, Model of hot-electron transport with SE-Auger generation and regeneration. SE-Auger recombination of a hybrid biexciton promotes an electron into a high-mobility transport band above the QD confinement barrier. During drift, the hot electron may partially relax into internal QD states, from which it can be re-excited into the transport band by SE-Auger energy transfer from a long-lived excited Mn ion, sustaining long-range transport. a.u., arbitrary units.

The complementary holes remain largely confined within the CdSe cores and are not expected to contribute appreciably to the fast TPC response. However, we do not detect persistent charge accumulation in the photoconductive gap, probably because the non-zero dark conductivity of the QD films (Extended Data Fig. 2) enables charge neutralization between successive excitation pulses.

Industry observers note that the measured TPC profiles are well described by the error-function form of the ToF expression for a Gaussian photoexcitation profile (dashed lines in Fig. 4a; Supplementary Note 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Minor deviations include an initial capacitive spike29,32 and a weak long-time tail associated with delayed electrons, discussed below.

Modelling of the d = 15 μm trace yields a drift velocity of vd = 24 μm ns−1 and an effective lifetime τ0 = 7 ns. In conventional ToF models, τ0 describes recombination and/or trapping of mobile carriers. Here it instead represents the effective lifetime of the high-mobility hot-electron population. Whereas hot electrons normally cool to the band edge within a few picoseconds14,33, in Mn-doped QDs, their lifetime is extended by SE-Auger regeneration (Fig. 4b). Long-lived Mn excitations persist during carrier transit and can repeatedly re-excite partially relaxed electrons into the transport band before complete cooling. Regeneration is imperfect, however: if a relaxing electron encounters a QD lacking an excited Mn ion or otherwise unable to support SE-Auger re-excitation, it relaxes into a low-mobility band-edge state. Thus, τ0 represents the average survival time of the regenerated hot-electron population.

ToF fits at longer transport distances yield an apparent decrease in vd from 24 μm ns−1 at d = 15 μm to 13 μm ns−1 at d = 65 μm, whereas τ0 remains essentially unchanged (Fig. 4a). We attribute this reduction to the increasing contribution of delayed electrons that progressively lose mobility as regeneration becomes less effective, broadening the trailing edge of the TPC transient. The shortest-distance value, vd = 24 μm ns−1, therefore provides the best estimate of the intrinsic drift velocity of the regenerated hot-electron population.

It has been revealed that we also estimate the transit time with the commonly used empirical approach, in which ttr is identified from the inflection point of a log–log TPC plot, determined from the intersection of power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions27,28,34,35 (Fig. 5a). The resulting ttr values scale linearly with d (Fig. 4a, inset), as expected for ToF transport. The slope yields vd = 21.5 ± 0.4 µm ns−1, in good agreement with the value obtained from error-function modelling of the d = 15 μm trace (vd = 24 µm ns−1).

At a lower bias (V = 70 V), ttr again scales linearly with d (Fig. 4a, inset and Extended Data Fig. 4), yielding vd = 15.3 ± 0.4 µm ns−1. The ratio of drift velocities at 70 V and 100 V (0.71) closely matches the voltage ratio (0.7), confirming the expected linear dependence of vd on electric field. Bias-dependent measurements at fixed distances (d = 45 µm and 25 µm; Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 5) provide an independent test: ttr increases with decreasing bias following the expected 1/V dependence (Fig. 5c).

a, Log–log plot of distance-dependent TPC traces measured for a heavily doped QD film at V = 100 V under 3.6-eV excitation with ⟨N⟩ = 5.12. The traces are vertically offset for clarity. Straight dashed lines show power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions of the uppermost TPC trace. Their intersection defines the carrier transit time ttr (red diamonds). b, Bias-dependent TPC traces measured at d = 45 µm under the same excitation conditions. Carrier transit times determined from the inflection points of the log–log traces are indicated by red diamonds. c, Transit time ttr versus bias V for d = 45 µm (open black squares) and 25 µm (filled red circles). Fits to ttr = (1/µe)(dL/V) yield electron mobilities of µe = 144 cm2 V−1 s−1 and 156 cm2 V−1 s−1, respectively. d, Transit time versus d/F combining distance-dependent (green and red symbols) and bias-dependent (black and blue symbols) measurements. The d/F axis is multiplied by 10 so that, with ttr in ns and d/F in µm2 V−1, the slope directly equals 1/µe for µe expressed in cm2 V−1 s−1. The data follow the expected linear dependence for ToF transport (line), yielding an average electron drift mobility of ⟨µe⟩ = 150 ± 11 cm2 V−1 s−1. The shaded region represents the one-standard-error uncertainty of the fitted mobility. a.u., arbitrary units.

According to recent reports, figure 5d summarizes all distance-dependent and bias-dependent measurements (25 data points) by plotting ttr versus d/F, with the horizontal axis scaled by a factor of 10 for convenient unit conversion, as described in the figure caption. For ToF transport, ttr = d/vd = (1/µ)(d/F), so the data should follow a straight line with slope 1/µ. The experimental data indeed collapse onto a single linear trend (Fig. 5d, black line), yielding an average electron mobility of ⟨µe⟩ = 150 ± 11 cm2 V−1 s−1, consistent with values obtained independently from the distance-dependent and bias-dependent data (Fig. 4a, inset and Fig. 5c).

Industry observers note that the ToF behaviour is reproducible across independently synthesized QD batches and several Auston switch devices. Further measurements yield electron mobilities of around 150–170 cm2 V−1 s−1 (Extended Data Fig. 6), confirming the robustness of the high-mobility hot-electron transport regime.

According to recent reports, although the present study focuses on 3.6-eV excitation, long-range hot-electron transport is also observed under near-band-edge excitation at 2.4 eV (Extended Data Fig. 7). In this case, the onset of the rapid TPC increase shifts from ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 to ⟨N⟩ ≈ 2, consistent with the SE-Auger ionization model. Because ejection of a near-band-edge electron requires two sequential SE-Auger upconversion steps, ionization occurs only once three excitons are generated, in agreement with previous observations of SE-driven photoionization2. Above this threshold, the transport characteristics are essentially unchanged: bias-dependent and distance-dependent TPC measurements exhibit the same ToF behaviour and yield ⟨μe⟩ = 164 cm2 V−1 s−1, close to the value obtained under 3.6-eV excitation.

The measured drift mobility, ⟨μe⟩ ≈ 150 cm2 V−1 s−1, is about an order of magnitude higher than values typically reported for strongly coupled, device-grade QD films (10–20 cm2 V−1 s−1) (refs. 1,36) and approaches the room-temperature electron drift mobilities of bulk wide-bandgap II–VI semiconductors (approximately 200–600 cm2 V−1 s−1) (ref. 37). This comparison serves only as a benchmark of mobility magnitude and does not imply equivalent transport mechanisms or device operation.

The high hot-electron mobility also enables long transport distances. Using τ0 = 7 ns and vd = 21.5 µm ns−1 (V = 100 V) gives a drift range of about 0.15 mm. Such transport distances are extraordinary for colloidal QD solids and place Mn-doped QD films in a transport regime more commonly associated with crystalline semiconductors than with ligand-linked nanocrystal assemblies. Collectively, these results demonstrate a high-mobility transport regime in which SE-Auger excitation promotes photoelectrons into a delocalized hot-carrier transport band, whereas repeated SE-Auger regeneration sustains their long-range drift (Fig. 4b).

According to recent reports, we report a phototransport regime in which SE-Auger upconversion dynamically promotes electrons into a delocalized, high-mobility band above the QD confinement barrier, yielding carrier mobilities of about 150 cm2 V−1 s−1 and submillimetre transport distances. Unlike conventional band-like transport, this mechanism does not rely on miniband formation or strong electronic coupling between neighbouring QDs. Instead, repeated SE-Auger activation regenerates high-energy transport states following partial relaxation, sustaining hot-electron transport over nanosecond timescales.

Long-range hot-electron transport can enable transit-time-limited photodetection in the GHz regime, ultrafast optical-to-electrical signal conversion and modulation and electrical sampling of ultrafast optical signals. Beyond optoelectronics, SE-enabled stabilization and transport of hot carriers offer a strategy for harnessing high-energy electrons in photochemical processes. Their high mobility, expanded wavefunctions and strong reducing power make them attractive as both energetic charge carriers and agents of remote chemical transformations.

Cadmium oxide (CdO, 99.99%, Aldrich), octadecylphosphonic acid (ODPA, 99%, PCI), trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO, 99%, Aldrich), trioctylphosphine (TOP, 97%, Aldrich), diphenylphosphine (DPP, 98%, Aldrich), selenium (Se, 200 mesh, 99.999%, Alfa Aesar), 1-octadecene (ODE, 90%, Aldrich), oleic acid (OA, 90%, Aldrich), oleylamine (OAm, 70%, Aldrich), manganese(II) acetate tetrahydrate (Mn(ac)2·4H2O, 99.999%, Strem) and tributylphosphine (TBP, 95%, Aldrich) were used as received.

CdSe core particles with a wurtzite crystal structure were synthesized following a previously reported method17. Specifically, 100 mg of CdO, 490 mg of ODPA and 5 g of TOPO were loaded into a three-neck flask and degassed under vacuum at 150 °C for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the mixture was heated to 320 °C and maintained at this temperature until it formed a clear solution. Subsequently, 1 ml of TOP was swiftly injected into the flask. After the temperature increased to 380 °C, 1 ml of a 1.4 M TOP–Se solution was rapidly injected. At this stage, 1 mol% of DPP was added to the TOP–Se solution to control the growth kinetics17. After 3 min, the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature by removing the heating mantle.

The resulting nanocrystals were collected by adding ethanol followed by centrifugation at 8,000 rpm. This washing procedure was repeated three times. The purified nanocrystals were then redispersed in toluene.

Sources indicate that to incorporate Mn into the synthesized CdSe nanocrystals, we used a diffusion-doping procedure16 following a refined protocol of ref. 17. To remove residual Cd species, the pre-synthesized CdSe nanocrystals dispersed in toluene were precipitated with ethanol. 75 mg of the precipitate was dissolved in a mixture of 27 ml of degassed ODE and 2.7 ml of OA. The mixture was heated to 60 °C under vacuum for 1 h. After cooling to room temperature, the nanocrystals were again precipitated with ethanol and collected by centrifugation at 8,000 rpm. The resulting precipitate was added to a mixture of 510 mg of Se, 3 ml of degassed ODE and 3 ml of TBP.

It has been revealed that separately, 90 mg of Mn(ac)2·4H2O, 45 ml of ODE, 1.8 ml of OA and 3.9 ml of OAm were loaded into a flask and degassed under vacuum at 100 °C for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the mixture was heated to 300 °C, after which the previously prepared CdSe nanocrystal/TBP–Se solution in ODE was swiftly injected. The reaction temperature was maintained at 300 °C and the doping level was controlled by the reaction time (typically 5–30 min). After completion of the reaction, the mixture was cooled to room temperature. Magnetic circular dichroism measurements indicated approximately 2–5 internal Mn2+ dopants per QD, depending on the doping time17.

Owing to the large abundance of surface trap states, as-prepared Mn-doped CdSe cores do not exhibit detectable PL. To suppress surface defects, the cores were coated with a CdS shell following procedures reported in ref. 17.

In a recent development, to prepare a Cd-oleate precursor solution, 123 mg of CdO, 2.45 ml of OA and 10.8 ml of ODE were loaded into a flask and degassed at 100 °C under vacuum for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the temperature was increased to 250 °C and maintained for 1 h until a clear solution formed. The precursor solution was then cooled to 100 °C and maintained at this temperature until injection during CdS shell growth.

A TOP–S precursor solution was prepared by stirring a mixture of 18 ml of TOP and 44.3 mg of sulfur powder overnight in a glovebox.

Sources indicate that for shell growth, 75 mg of Mn-doped CdSe QDs were dissolved in a mixture of 28 ml of ODE, 2.4 ml of OAm and 1.2 ml of OA. This mixture was degassed at 100 °C under vacuum for 1 h. Under nitrogen flow, the flask was heated to 220 °C and 0.4-ml aliquots of the Cd-oleate and TOP–S precursor solutions were alternately injected dropwise at intervals of 2.5 min for two cycles.

A 100-nm gold layer was evaporated onto the backside of a 1-mm glass substrate to serve as the ground plane. An approximately 200-nm-thick film of undoped (reference) or Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs was then deposited on the top surface of the substrate through repeated spin-coating cycles, accompanied by ligand exchange and rinsing steps. During deposition, QDs dispersed in octane (20 mg ml−1) were spin-coated at 1,600 rpm for 30 s.

To facilitate interdot charge transport, the QDs were cross-linked by means of solid-state ligand exchange, replacing the original long-chain ligands with short bifunctional 1,2-ethanedithiol (EDT) molecules. For ligand exchange, 60 µl of a 1 M EDT solution in methanol (MeOH) was dropped onto the QD layer, allowed to soak for 60 s and then spin-coated at 1,200 rpm for 30 s.

The film was subsequently rinsed by spin-coating pure MeOH to remove excess ligands. These three steps—QD deposition, ligand exchange and rinsing—were repeated five times to obtain a QD layer approximately 200 nm thick. The resulting film was annealed at 150 °C for 30 min.

Finally, two 200-nm-thick gold contacts separated by a 70-µm gap were deposited on top of the QD film through a shadow mask. Together with the gold ground plane on the backside of the substrate, these contacts form a microstrip transmission line with a nominal impedance of 50 Ω.

It has been revealed that to verify that ligand exchange and film fabrication preserved the quantum-confined electronic structure of the QDs, we performed further TA measurements on 200-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD films prepared using the same ligand-exchange procedure as used for the TPC devices. The TA spectra of the film samples were compared with those of the corresponding QDs in solution under identical excitation conditions (3.6-eV, 150-fs excitation; ⟨N⟩ = 0.3). The results are presented in Extended Data Fig. 8.

Industry observers note that to characterize the equilibrium electrical properties of the ligand-exchanged QD films, further dark-conductivity measurements were performed using 120-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD films deposited on glass substrates and contacted by thermally evaporated interdigitated Au electrodes comprising 25 pairs of 2-mm-long fingers separated by 10 μm. The corresponding current–voltage characteristics are presented in Extended Data Fig. 2.

According to recent reports, electrostatic simulations of the Auston switch geometry were performed using the Electrostatics interface of COMSOL Multiphysics to calculate the electric-field distribution, effective gap capacitance and effective RC constant (Extended Data Fig. 1).

TA measurements were performed using a standard pump–probe set-up in which absorption changes induced by a short pump pulse were probed in both the temporal and spectral domains using variably delayed probe pulses. The TA system was built around a regeneratively amplified ytterbium-doped potassium gadolinium tungstate (Yb:KGW) femtosecond laser (PHAROS, Light Conversion) generating approximately 190-fs pulses at 1.2 eV.

In a recent development, the laser output was split into two beams. One beam seeded a harmonic generator (HIRO HHG, Light Conversion) to produce second (2.4-eV) or third (3.6-eV) harmonic pump pulses, whose duration was shortened to about 150 fs owing to nonlinear optical pulse compression. Pulses from the second beam were delayed relative to the pump using an optical delay line (up to 5 ns) and focused onto a 3-mm-thick sapphire plate to generate broadband probe pulses in the form of a femtosecond white-light continuum.

In a recent development, the pump beam was focused onto the sample into a spot with a diameter of about 120 µm, whereas the smaller-diameter probe beam (<90 µm) was centred near the middle of the pump spot. Probe pulses transmitted through the sample were detected using an Avantes AvaSpec-Fast ULS1350F-USB2 spectrometer. The measured TA spectra were corrected for chirp (spectrally dependent delay within the white-light continuum probe pulses) using the procedure described in ref. 2.

In Auger recombination studies of undoped and Mn-doped QDs, we monitored the pump-induced band-edge absorption bleach (ΔαBE), which tracks the decay of band-edge excitonic populations14.

To minimize sample degradation during TPC measurements, the fabricated Auston switch devices were mounted in a nitrogen-filled, airtight chamber equipped with optical windows and electrical feedthroughs. Under these conditions, no measurable changes in the TPC response were observed during the complete characterization of a device, including pump-fluence-dependent, transport-distance-dependent and bias-dependent measurements.

Industry observers note that the chamber was mounted on a translation stage, allowing the laser beam position within the electrode gap to be varied. One of the top gold electrodes was biased using a DC power supply (Keithley 2430), whereas the other electrode was connected to a 20-GHz-bandwidth sampling oscilloscope by means of a coaxial cable. To minimize timing jitter, the oscilloscope was triggered by electrical pulses generated by a high-speed Si photodetector driven by a portion of the laser beam split from the excitation path.

Industry observers note that the QDs within the photoconductive gap of the Auston switch were excited at 2.4 eV or 3.6 eV using 150-fs pulses of the second or third harmonic of an amplified Yb:KGW femtosecond PHAROS laser, respectively. The laser beam was focused with a cylindrical achromatic lens into a narrow stripe aligned with the edges of the top gold electrodes. The spatial profile of the excitation beam was approximately Gaussian, with a stripe width of about 70–80 µm (FWHM), measured with a beam profiler. The excitation position within the photoconductive gap of the Auston switch was varied by translating the sample in a plane perpendicular to the laser beam. The position was initially calibrated using a beam profiler and monitored in real time on the sample with a CMOS camera.

As discussed in Supplementary Note 3, the nonlinear dependence of SE-Auger upconversion on excitation density narrows the lateral spatial profile of the mobile hot-electron population relative to the laser beam profile (Extended Data Fig. 9). Across the film thickness, the initial hot-electron population is weighted towards the illuminated surface. However, because the optical absorption length is comparable with the QD film thickness, excited Mn ions are generated throughout the layer. Consequently, SE-Auger regeneration remains active across the film thickness, even if the hot-electron population spreads vertically during transit within the photoconductive gap.

Industry observers note that a, Top view of the modelled structure consisting of a 200-nm-thick Mn-doped QD film deposited on a 1-mm-thick glass substrate with two 2-mm-wide and 200-nm-thick gold (Au) electrodes separated by a 70-μm gap. The static dielectric constants of the QD film and glass substrate were taken as 6.0 and 4.1, respectively. b, Cross-sectional view showing the calculated electrostatic potential (colour map) and electric-field lines for an applied bias of V = 100 V, obtained using the Electrostatics module of COMSOL Multiphysics. c,d, Calculated horizontal (Ex) and vertical (Ez) electric-field components in the QD film as a function of the distance from the positive electrode. The vertical electric field is negligible over nearly the entire photoconductive gap and becomes appreciable only within approximately 1 μm of the electrode edges. By contrast, the horizontal electric field remains nearly uniform across the gap, with an average value within 10–15% of the nominal field F = V/L. These calculations confirm that the electric field is predominantly horizontal, thereby validating the one-dimensional drift approximation used in the charge transport analysis. The computed electrostatic field distribution yields an effective gap capacitance of approximately 0.2 pF, corresponding to an estimated RC time constant of 10 ps for a 50-Ω transmission line. This value is shorter than the experimental temporal resolution of the TPC measurements (about 50 ps), indicating that the measured response is limited not by the device RC constant but by other components of the measurement circuit and the oscilloscope.

The measurements were performed on a 120-nm-thick Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QD film deposited on a glass substrate and contacted by thermally evaporated interdigitated Au electrodes comprising 25 pairs of 2-mm-long fingers separated by 10 μm. The measured current exhibits a linear dependence on the applied bias over the investigated voltage range (±60 V), corresponding to maximum electric fields of approximately 6 V μm−1, about four times larger than those used in the TPC experiments. The absence of measurable nonlinearity indicates no detectable contact-limited (Schottky) behaviour under these conditions. The extracted film resistivity is approximately 2.2 × 1010 Ω cm, demonstrating that the ligand-exchanged QD films are highly insulating at equilibrium and therefore contain only a negligible concentration of free carriers.

Sources indicate that simulated photocurrent transients for a Gaussian spatial distribution of photogenerated carriers, using an effective lifetime of τ0 = 10 ns for illustration. In the absence of charge transit (vd = 0, black line; top inset), the photocurrent decays only through carrier loss with time constant τ0. For a non-zero drift velocity (bottom inset), the transient develops a cut-off when the carrier packet reaches the collecting electrode (the positive contact in the present case, assuming electron-dominated photocurrent). Blue and red traces correspond to vd = 10 µm ns−1 and d = 45 µm (blue line), vd = 20 µm ns−1 and d = 45 µm (solid red line) and vd = 20 µm ns−1 and d = 25 µm (dashed red line). Here d is the distance from the centre of the initial carrier distribution to the charge-collecting electrode and vd is the drift velocity. a.u., arbitrary units.

According to recent reports, TPC traces measured as a function of the transport distance from the positive electrode (d) at a fixed applied bias of 70 V (solid lines) under 3.6-eV, 150-fs excitation at an excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 5.12. Dashed straight lines show power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions of the top TPC trace. The intersection of these lines defines the carrier transit time (ttr), indicated by red diamonds. a.u., arbitrary units.

TPC traces measured at a fixed transport distance of d = 25 μm under 3.6-eV, 150-fs excitation at an excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 5.12 (solid lines). Carrier transit times (ttr), determined from the inflection points of the log–log TPC traces, are indicated by diamonds. The inflection points were obtained from the intersections of power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions (dashed black lines). a.u., arbitrary units.

An extra batch of Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs was synthesized independently, incorporated into a separate Auston switch device and measured using excitation with 150-fs, 3.6-eV laser pulses at ⟨N⟩ ≈ 5. a, Distance-dependent TPC traces recorded at V = 100 V. The carrier transit time (ttr, indicated by red diamonds) increases with the transport distance (d), as expected for ToF transport. b, Bias-dependent TPC traces measured at d = 25 μm. The measured transit time increases with decreasing V, again consistent with ToF transport. c, Transit time plotted as a function of 10d/F, in which F is the applied electric field, using the data from panels a (blue diamonds) and b (red circles). The factor of 10 is introduced for convenient conversion of the fitted slope to mobility in cm2 V−1 s−1, as described in Fig. 5d. The linear fit (dashed line) yields an average electron mobility of ⟨μe⟩ = 170.6 cm2 V−1 s−1, consistent with the value reported in the main text (Fig. 5d). a.u., arbitrary units.

In a recent development, a, Early-time TPC amplitude as a function of the average number of excitons per QD, ⟨N⟩, measured using 2.4-eV, 150-fs excitation pulses (black squares). For comparison, corresponding data obtained with 3.6-eV excitation are shown by red circles. The onset of the rapid TPC increase shifts from ⟨N⟩ ≈ 1 for 3.6-eV excitation to ⟨N⟩ ≈ 2 for 2.4-eV excitation, consistent with hot-electron generation by means of single-step and two-step SE-Auger upconversion, respectively. This behaviour is expected because ejection of a cold band-edge electron requires an energy of approximately 3.5 eV, which exceeds the energy released in a single SE-Auger event (about 2.1 eV) and therefore requires two sequential SE-mediated upconversion steps. b, Bias-dependent TPC traces (log–log representation) measured at a fixed transport distance of d = 25 μm and ⟨N⟩ ≈ 4. Carrier transit times (ttr), determined from power-law fits to the pre-transit and post-transit regions, are indicated by the red diamonds. c, Distance-dependent TPC traces measured at an applied bias of 100 V. Transit times are indicated by the red diamonds. d, Transit time plotted as a function of 10 d/F, in which F is the applied electric field, obtained from the data in panels b (red circles) and c (blue diamonds). The factor of 10 is introduced for convenient conversion of the fitted slope to mobility in cm2 V−1 s−1, as described in Fig. 5d. The linear fit (line) yields an average electron mobility of ⟨μe⟩ = 164 cm2 V−1 s−1, demonstrating that long-range, high-mobility transport is preserved under near-band-edge excitation. a.u., arbitrary units.

In a recent development, comparison of early-time TA spectra of Mn-doped CdSe/CdS QDs measured in solution (1-mm optical path length) and in a 200-nm-thick solid-state film prepared using the same ligand-exchange procedure as used in the TPC experiments. The measurements were performed under identical excitation conditions: 3.6-eV, 150-fs pump pulses at an average excitation level of ⟨N⟩ = 0.3 and a pump–probe delay of Δt = 4 ps. In both samples, the band-edge bleach is centred at 2.35 eV, demonstrating that ligand exchange and film processing preserve the QD bandgap and, therefore, the quantum-confinement regime without evidence of QD sintering. The broader bleach observed in the film sample is attributed to the lower signal-to-noise ratio resulting from the much smaller optical density of the 200-nm film, which partially obscures the two closely spaced transitions involving the same 1Se electron level and the 1Sh,3/2 and 2Sh,3/2 hole states.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool lost their 100% record in this season’s Champions League with defeat at Fenerbahce three weeks ago, and they’ll be aiming to bounce back tonight with victory away to Club Brugge.

For Reds fans of a certain vintage, the Belgian outfit will evoke happy memories of the triumphant 1976 UEFA Cup final and 1978 European Cup final, with this being the first meeting since the latter success at Wembley.

Andoni Iraola’s satisfaction at Sunday’s 4-0 drubbing of Manchester United has been tempered by ongoing injuries to Cody Gakpo and Ryan Gravenberch, with no return date set for the midfielder  as he continues to struggle with a heel problem.

The Liverpool head coach spoke of how he ‘enjoyed analysing’ Club Brugge, who go into this game level on points and goal difference with the Reds and have a red-hot striker in Nicolo Tresoldi, who’s already netted 16 times this season (including a hat-trick against Inter Milan).

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Iraola has made three changes from the starting XI which thumped Man United on Sunday.

Alisson Becker continues between the sticks, and there’s one change to the defence. It’s a surprising one, too, with Virgil van Dijk omitted from the line-up to allow for the reintroduction of Jeremie Frimpong at right-back.

Ronald Araujo duly shuffles across to centre-back to partner Jeremy Jacquet, with Milos Kerkez on the left.

One alteration in midfield sees Trey Nyoni come in for Alexis Mac Allister, with the teenager lining up next to Dominik Szoboszlai.

The third and final change to the starting XI sees Victor Munoz replace Rio Ngumoha in attack, with Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak all keeping their places.

The trio who are cut from the line-up are all on the substitutes’ bench, which also includes a mixture of youth (Jayden Danns, James McConnell, Lewis Koumas, Luke Chambers) and experience (Joe Gomez, Kostas Tsimikas, Freddie Woodman).

You can view the Liverpool starting XI and substitutes below, via @LFC on X:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 10:27.
  • Bournemouth have prepared for their Europa League clash at Celta Vigo in the knowledge that they could smash even more history.
  • Marco Rose's side won just two of their opening eight competitive matches of the 2026-27 season, hinting that there could be a period of struggle following Andoni Iraola's departure to Liverpool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Carter White | 26 Nov 2026 10:27.

Bournemouth have prepared for their Europa League clash at Celta Vigo in the knowledge that they could smash even more history.

Marco Rose's side won just two of their opening eight competitive matches of the 2026-27 season, hinting that there could be a period of struggle following Andoni Iraola's departure to Liverpool.

However, with the Cherries set for a Celta Vigo challenge on Thursday night, it is clear that the Dean Court club are thriving, with the visitors to Spain sitting in fifth position in the Premier League standings.

A star of the current positive form, Evanilson has truly announced himself as an elite top-flight striker, netting seven goals and providing two assists in his past eight appearances, scoring in five consecutive league fixtures.

What makes Bournemouth's run even more impressive is that last season's star man Junior Kroupi has barely started a competitive match so far after recovering from a broken leg sustained over the summer.

Starting with a 3-0 Europa League success over Austrian side Sturm Graz on October 15, Bournemouth have recorded nine straight victories in all competitions across the Premier League, EFL Cup and European action.

That winning streak is the longest since the Cherries became a Football League club at the beginning of the 1923-24 season, showcasing how impressively the South Coast team are performing at the moment.

However, there are still more records to be achieved over the coming weeks, with Bournemouth aiming to become only the eighth team to record 10 straight competitive victories whilst playing in the Premier League.

Winning the Premier League during the 2016-17 campaign under Antonio Conte, Chelsea managed 10 wins in a row in all competitions, with that particular streak running from October 2016 until Latest Year's Eve 2016.

Leeds are the other club to post that exact number of wins in succession, with the Elland Road side completing the feat between August and October during the 1999-00 Premier League term.

The dominant force in English domestic football during the late 2010s and early 2020s, Manchester City are unsurprisingly the club with the most consecutive competitive wins as a Premier League side.

Under the expert stewardship of Pep Guardiola, the title-winning Citizens won 21 straight matches between December 2020 and March 2021, destroying Arsenal's previous record of 13 games in succession.

To match Man City's record, Bournemouth would need to secure victory in Spain on Thursday before winning every single match up to and including the trip to Brighton & Hove Albion on January 5.

Relive Daily Mail Sport's coverage of Tuesday's Champions League action as Arsenal clashed with Borussia Dortmund and Manchester City took on Napoli.

Right, it's time for me to head off.

It was not a good night for the Premier League sides in the Champions League. Three teams played; none won.

According to recent reports, aston Villa kicked the evening off with a disappointing defeat away at Galatasaray, with the backing track of whistling to make it an even more miserable day for them. I can still hear it in my ears.

And then it was the turn of both Arsenal and Manchester City to struggle...

Arsenal dominated Borussia Dortmund from minute one to 90, even going 1-0 up, but somehow left the Emirates with just an extra point on the board.

Anyway, I'm heading off now. Thanks for joining, and we will see you tomorrow night.

Arsenal's winning run at the Emirates is over.

Industry observers note that they had been on a mental run of wins at home in both the Champions League and Europa League. Like, I mean truly crazy. But now it's come to an end.

They have failed to win a home game in the group stage of major European competition for the first time since November 2019 (2-1 defeat vs Eintracht Frankfurt). Yep, seven years... told you it was mental.

Tonight's draw ends a run of 18 successive victories – the longest such winning run by any side in major European competition history.

I bet Borussia Dortmund just can't wait to get out of London.

Tonight is yet another evening where they have struggled playing in England - they never seem to do well here.

Recent findings suggest that never mind the lack of an ice vest, George Russell is somehow going to need to be the coolest man in Malaysia if he is to turn seventh on the grid into a positive result in Sunday’s Bahrain Grand Prix.The first race in Sepang in nearly a decade – a late addition to the calendar because of the conflict in the Middle East – promises to be an absolute scorcher. It might even be worth setting your alarm for the 8am UK start time. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will start in pole position for the first time this year. He will have Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton alongside him.

It will be the first time since Hungary 2023 that those two gladiators have started on a front row together. Throw in sweltering temperatures, low grip, high tyre degradation, and the ever-present threat of a Malaysian monsoon sweeping through Sepang, and you have the potential for fireworks.

Sources indicate that russell might need something wacky if he is to do anything from that far back. This was a desperately disappointing result for the British driver. After his victory in Baku last weekend, Russell was hopeful he had finally found the winning formula and that he could continue to take the fight to his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, whom he trails in the drivers’ championship by 66pts.

Eighth, four places behind, and 0.24sec slower than the Italian, was not what Russell would have had in mind, although both Mercedes drivers will rise a spot because of the five-place grid penalty meted out to Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar for exceeding his engine allowance for the season.Russell will have felt particularly disappointed as Antonelli only got one run in Q3 after using up a set of soft tyres when he made a mistake and went off track in Q2. He now trails his team mate nine-seven in qualifying head-to-head this year.“No to be honest,” Russell admitted when asked whether he knew why he was so slow. “This circuit is an outlier in terms of the abrasiveness of the tarmac.“The lap times seven years ago were six or seven seconds faster and at certain points on the track it feels like you are driving on gravel, which is the same for everyone, but it is clearly affecting us more than others.”Mercedes’ lack of performance was doubly unexpected because not only did they arrive here with a massive upgrade package, but Russell revealed this week that he and Antonelli were foregoing the cooling vests you see some drivers sporting on the grid, in favour of car performance.

Toto Wolff, the Mercedes team principal, admitted it was a head-scratcher. “Very difficult to understand,” the Austrian remarked. “We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we did not see all year, but then you can say it is very hot and the tarmac is different to all the [other] tracks. It looked really good this morning. We seemed to have, at least with Kimi, made a step in understanding. And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”.

Still, both titles are in the bag so Wolff cannot be too unhappy. Russell is the one who will be really miffed. He really needs to be beating his team-mate pretty much every race weekend if he is to get his title hopes back on track.

At the front, the mood was somewhat different. Verstappen became the first non-Mercedes-powered pilot to take a pole position this year. It was a first pole position for Red Bull Powertrains, too. And with his long run pace looking more than decent, Verstappen should really hold on for his first win of 2026. Hamilton will do his best to hang on to the Dutchman’s coattails. The seven-time champion was delighted when told he had taken P2. “Let’s go guys! Finally! Great job guys, really great job. Car felt great.”.

This was indeed an excellent performance from the Ferrari man – and just the tonic for the Scuderia after weeks of gossip and speculation. Hamilton was admittedly three tenths slower than his rival, which he put purely down to a power deficit on the straights, but he noted he was hopeful his long run pace was more competitive. The last time a F1 held a race was held here back in 2017, the British driver claimed pole only to be overhauled by a youthful Verstappen. He will be desperate to turn the tables this time.

“It was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one change before qualifying and we hit the sweet spot,” he reflected afterwards. “I am so, so grateful. I will try my best to hold on to Max tomorrow, and if we are in the fight that would be awesome. I’ve been talking too much, but I guess you talk more when you are happy. It was my best lap of the year. It feels like I won, and I will give it everything tomorrow.”.

It is Russell, though, who needs a result even more badly if he is to remain a factor in the championship. “As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us,” he admitted, adding that “all the numbers” from the upgrade package suggested it was an improvement on the old car. “But I think there is going to be a lot happening tomorrow. The tyre deg is huge and race pace will be king. So even though today was a real disappointment it is not the be all and end all.”.

No. 1 ☝️#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/01PqrckQS9.

And then, qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”.

On Kimi Antonelli’s track limits breach in Q2:.

“Not good, because Q2 you know you are going to get through. You lose a set [of softs] in a qualifying that is so tight, where we are on the back foot. That is not good.”.

According to recent reports, lewis Hamilton states this is the biggest crowd he has ever seen at Sepang, thanking the fans for making it here today. That is actually a bigger compliment than many watching at home may realise. The traffic this weekend has been horrendous. After 10 years without a race in Malaysia, during which time F1 has grown massively, I think they have forgotten how to do traffic management. Shuttles are inconsistent, taxis can’t get in/out, it’s taking forever just to reach the airport a few kilometres away - some fans have been braving the heat and walking. It took over two hours to get back into Kuala Lumpur last night (48km). My understanding is the Bahrainis are organising the race this year, while local forces are handling the traffic outside the circuit.

Sources indicate that “The car has been very good since last week. It is good to come back [from his wrist injury] at such a time and I am enjoying it, fighting for the top three. Even though it was not my finest qualifying session it is a good feeling.

“It is a bit unfortunate we take a penalty on a track where we are that fast but, from eighth, I am confident we can come through the field and come back for a good result.”.

“I love this energy [from the crowd]. Substantial, big thank you to Malaysia for welcoming us. It is so hot here. I keep saying it, but that has made it a massive challenge for the tyres, the car, the mechanics in the garage. I am really, really thankful to my team. We made so many changes through all these practice sessions. Because the cars are sliding, the tyres are overheating, it was really hard to find a good balance, and we made one last change going into qualifying and I think we hit the sweet spot. To be able to close the gap to two or three tenths to Max [Verstappen], who has been so quick all weekend, is great, and I am so grateful.

“I am much happier with where the car is, but tomorrow is a completely different ballgame. Making these tyres last around this track, they are overheating from the get-go. Every little bit of wheelspin you have, every little snap you have makes a difference of how far you are going to go. I like to think we have got a good balance. Max was really quick on his long runs, so I will just try my best to hold onto him tomorrow.”.

A reminder that Isack Hadjar will drop from third to eighth after his grid penalty.

Recent findings suggest that big disappointment that for Russell. After his win in Baku, where he stated he finally felt hooked up to the car, he was desperate to build the momentum. P8, four places behind Antonelli, was not what he would have had in mind. Has it all to do in the race tomorrow.

Excellent (though not unexpected) pole for Verstappen, and a very good P2 for Hamilton. Could be some fireworks on the front row tomorrow.

The screens in the media centre here in Sepang tell me that the air temp right now is 32.8C and the track temp is 58C. It feels even hotter. Lots of chat about cooling vests this week, which are optional. George Russell is among the drivers who isn’t using one, which is interesting a) because Russell has suffered badly from heat in the past (Qatar, Singapore) and b) because he indicates Mercedes chose to put the development money into car upgrades instead.

It has been revealed that it’s an interesting admission. Not everyone is sold on the idea of cooling vests. Ferrari and McLaren will definitely be using them this weekend, for instance. Max Verstappen won’t as he doesn’t like them. Russell thinks the FIA should just develop the tech themselves and it shouldn’t be part of the budget cap.

“Our team have put a lot of emphasis this year on the cockpit temperature,” he remarked. “We won’t be running the cooling vest because we haven’t put the resource into making it robust enough. I feel we need the FIA just to step in and say ‘Here’s some money extra in the cost cap or there’s an external firm who’s going to develop it for everybody’. Because we should all be wearing it. When it works, it works great. So, I would like to wear it this week, and I would like to wear it next week. But the team asked me...look, we can develop it, and we can put the money towards it...[but at a cost].

Sources indicate that he added: “The top itself is not expensive ..you’ve got to effectively make a system where you can fit a block of dry ice or actual ice, and then has the airflow to circulate the cool water throughout. If that system isn’t robust enough, then suddenly you have no circulation, and then you get hot. You get ambient temperature circulating. The vest is one-design, but the system that circulates the water is different [at different teams].”.

Sources indicate that ferrari this week have publicly backed their team principal Frederic Vasseur, amid speculation over the Frenchman’s position and comments made by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, who said the job at Ferrari would be a “dream job”. Ferrari, who sit second in the constructors’ standings, have not won the drivers’ championship since 2007 (Kimi Raikkonen) and the constructors’ since 2008. Here is a snippet from Tom Cary’s piece on the matter:.

In a hastily convened media call on Tuesday morning, Maria Conti, Ferrari’s chief communication officer, said the Scuderia had decided to matter a vote of confidence in Vasseur in response “not just to the story of Mr Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred”.

Recent findings suggest that “Ferrari has made its choices,” Conti remarked. “We have confidence – full confidence – in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so.

“At this time, it’s really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.”.

“It is great to be back [in Malaysia]. I am really enjoying the track. We have had some wonderful races here over time. It is actually the 20th time we have been here, it started in 1999, and it is really exciting to be back. I really enjoyed getting out on the track and watching the cars closely.

In a recent development, “The drivers are super fit and they have some cooling but it is not easy. But you almost cannot get enough fluid through your body before your stomach gives up. Having this race and Singapore back-to-back increases that challenge.”.

Especially with the big upgrade they have brought this weekend, Mercedes’ lead at the summit is looking unassailable right now.

Sources indicate that almost nine years ago to the day, Max Verstappen took just his second race victory in Formula 1. Lewis Hamilton, who took pole position, and Daniel Ricciardo joined Verstappen on the podium. Despite being nine years ago, plenty of drivers still on the grid were racing that weekend. According to recent reports, with Russell winning in Baku and Antonelli finishing fifth, the latter’s championship lead was cut to 66 points. If Russell is going to usurp his teammate, he is going to need a few more similar results to last weekend due to the size of Antonelli’s lead. If Antonelli were to suffer a retirement, then that completely changes the outlook.

Recent findings suggest that formula One returns to Malaysia for round 16 of the season for the Bahrain Grand Prix. That probably sounds strange but after the Bahrain Grand Prix was originally postponed in March, F1 reinstated it to the calendar with Malaysia hosting it because of the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite being held in Malaysia, Bahrain have retained the naming rights for the event, which is officially known as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. The last time Formula One was in Malaysia was nine years ago back in 2017, when a young whippersnapper named Max Verstappen, still four years away from winning his first world championship, claimed just his second victory.

In a recent development, last time out around the streets of Baku, Mercedes’ George Russell claimed victory at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, pipping Verstappen by just a tenth of a second. That was Russell’s first grand prix win since June and cuts his team-mate Kimi Antonelli’s lead in the drivers’ standings to 66 points. Antonelli had a challenging weekend in Baku, starting 16th after a crash in qualifying and coming home in fifth to see his championship lead to Russell cut by 15 points.

Recent findings suggest that verstappen was quickest in first practice yesterday, with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc fastest in second practice. Earlier today, championship leader Antonelli was nearly three tenths clear of the field in third practice. Mercedes, 160 points clear at the top of the constructors’ standings, have brought significant upgrades this weekend, which includes a upcoming floor, rear suspension and rear corner. It is the team’s first significant car update since the Canadian Grand at the end of May.

Recent findings suggest that this race in Malaysia represents the second leg of the season’s first flyaway triple header, with the Singapore Grand Prix to come next weekend, so the demands on the teams and the drivers are incredibly high. Qualifying from Sepang gets under way at 9am (GMT).

This evening, AC Milan have been dealt some good and bad injury news ahead of their game against Olympiacos.

It’s been a particularly unfortunate season for Milan where injuries are involved, and today, they have suffered a newly introduced problem in midfield, with Luka Modric out of this week’s crucial game in the Europa League.

It has been revealed that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Recent findings suggest that milanNews relays a report from Sky, and it’s best to start with the bad news: Modric has suffered ‘a muscle strain in his right rectus femoris’. The Croatian will definitely miss this week’s game against the Greek outfit and the game against Cagliari is in doubt.

However, he should be back for the game against Parma. It offers a significant chance for Ardon Jashari to potentially step up, especially after his goal at the weekend. Nevertheless, it brings up questions about who is fit to actually replace the Croatian in the squad.

It’s not all bad news, though. The report also confirms that Fikayo Tomori will be back in full training tomorrow, alongside the group. Amorim had hoped to have him back for the win against Frosinone, so whether he’ll play on Thursday remains to be seen.

In a recent development, nevertheless, it’s a welcome boost, especially with the news of Pavlovic’s upcoming check-up. Of course, with that check-up, he’s expected to miss Thursday’s game as well.

By Calum Burrowes | 26 Nov 2026 10:55, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 20:05.

Two former Arsenal teammates come head to head on Saturday in League One as in-form Luton Town welcome high-flying Oxford United to Kenilworth Road.

Jack Wilshere's side will be looking to extend their unbeaten run to nine matches in all competitions after coming from behind to win 2-1 last weekend, while Aaron Ramsey and his U's will be aiming to move into the automatic promotion places by securing a fourth win in five third-tier outings.

More than six months after Luton Town narrowly missed out on a place in the League One playoffs last season, finishing just one point behind sixth-placed Leyton Orient, the Hatters have made a positive start to the 2026-27 campaign as they look to go one step better this time around.

Wilshere's side began the newly introduced season inconsistently and were sitting 16th after seven third-tier matches at the end of September, but have since enjoyed an impressive upturn in form, losing just once in the league across October and November, a 2-1 defeat to MK Dons at Stadium MK.

That run has seen Luton win six of their last eight league matches, while also progressing to the second round of the FA Cup and the knockout stages of the EFL Trophy, putting them firmly back in the playoff picture.

In fact, the Hatters could move into second place heading into the final month of the calendar year if they secure a ninth league victory of the season and other results go their way this weekend, with their recent form having lifted them more than 10 places into fifth and guaranteed them a place in the top six until at least their 17th league match next week, when they face struggling Blackpool.

A key factor behind their turnaround has been an improvement in front of goal, with Luton scoring 17 times in League One since the start of October, an average of more than two per game that has taken their overall tally to 29, a record bettered by just one side in the division.

As for the visitors, Oxford United make the 66-mile journey to Bedfordshire in similarly strong form and will be looking to move into December in the top two by recording a third consecutive victory.

The U's, led by former Wales midfielder Ramsey, have enjoyed a more consistent campaign than their upcoming opponents, having already moved into the top six by their seventh match of the 2026-27 season, when Luton were sitting 16th, and have continued to build on that strong start in recent weeks to climb to third.

Oxford head into their 15th league outing of the season with 29 points following eight wins, five draws and just one defeat, and they could move level on points with leaders Stockport County this weekend while still having two games in hand on Jimmy McNulty's side.

Although Oxford's FA Cup campaign came to an end at the first hurdle with a 1-0 home defeat to Stevenage, their form in the third tier has been exceptional, with no side in the top four divisions of English football losing fewer league matches than the U's.

Only Ramsey and Wilshere's former club Arsenal and League Two side Barnet have matched their tally of just one defeat.

While Luton have built their campaign around a clinical attacking unit, Oxford's promotion push has been underpinned by a strong defensive record, with only three sides in League One having conceded fewer than their 14 goals.

However, shipping three at home to Wycombe Wanderers last weekend, despite coming from three goals behind to secure a remarkable 4-3 victory, represented a rare blemish on an otherwise impressive defensive campaign.

The pair meet for the first time in just under two years on Saturday and will lock horns in a third-tier fixture for the first time since 2019, with Luton having enjoyed a spell in the Premier League since their previous meeting at this level.

Luton Town form (all competitions):.

Oxford United form (all competitions):.

Luton Town will be forced into at least one change following their weekend victory over Burton Albion after Jordan Clark was forced off with an injury in the 33rd minute, with the midfielder expected to miss out and potentially be replaced by Daniel Gore.

Clark is set to join fellow injury absentees Hakeem Odoffin, Gideon Kodua and Shayden Morris in the treatment room, with the latter yet to feature at all this season.

Former Bristol City forward Nahki Wells marked his 15th league appearance of the campaign with his eighth and ninth goals of the season, scoring a brace against the Brewers last Saturday, and the Bermudian is expected to lead the line once again.

Having been in EFL Trophy action during the week, beating Tottenham Hotspur Under-21s 2-1, Ramsey is expected to make wholesale changes for Oxford's return to League One action.

Jamie Cumming started in goal for the midweek cup tie and could retain his place ahead of Simon Eastwood, who conceded three times last weekend, while changes are also expected throughout the defence, midfield and attack.

Gatlin O'Donkor came off the bench to score a dramatic winner five minutes into stoppage time against Wycombe and could therefore be rewarded with a starting place on Saturday, potentially at the expense of Tyler Goodrham.

Luton Town possible starting lineup:.

Shea; Jones, Mengi, Andersen, Johnston; Walsh; Richards, Donley, Gore, Palmer; Wells.

Oxford United possible starting lineup:.

Cumming; Kioso, Long, Brown, Currie; Brannagan, Andrews; Missanga, O'Donkor, Emakhu; Harris.

While Oxford United arrive at Kenilworth Road in high spirits, they face a side who have collected more points than any other team in the division across their last six league games, meaning the U's will know they face a difficult task to win at a ground where they have not tasted victory since 2017.

With that said, Oxford did manage to come away from their last visit to Luton with a point, albeit more than two years ago, and we expect them to repeat that feat, with the two in form sides playing out a 2-2 draw.
